sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Lahmu** (*lahmu*) ​— Primordial ‌Being · ‌The hairy ​one — ​belongs to ​the Mesopotamian ​tradition, where ​it is ‌catalogued under ​the domain ​"Primordial Being". ‌The name ​means "The ‌hairy one"[^1].

​**Lahmu** is ‌the Mesopotamian ​primordial being ​whose name ​simply means ​'the hairy ​one'. In ‌the *Enuma ​Elish* he ‌is the ​firstborn of ‌Apsû and ​Tiāmat, the ‌earliest divine ​generation before ‌sky and ​earth were ​fixed. Beyond ‌cosmogony, he ‌is a ‌protective spirit: ​a bearded, ​hair-covered guardian ‌posted at ​doorways, gates, ​and thresholds ‌to turn ​aside demons ​and pollution.

‌He stands ​at the ‌border between ​chaos and ​order — ​born from ​the mingled ‌primordial waters, ‌then stationed ​at the ‌doors that ​keep the ​ordered world ‌safe.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores the ‌name as ‌**Lahmu** and ​serves its ‌temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/lahmu/). ​The restoration ​needs no ‌distinctive letters ​or diacritics ​its ASCII ​form would ‌lose, which ​places the ​name in ​Tier 2. ‌The plain ​ASCII form ‌*lahmu* survives ​as a ‌modern convenience ​imposed by ‌the early ‌domain-name system; ​the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Cuneiform ​as ​**𒀭𒌓𒈬**. Etymologically ​it ​means ‌"The ​hairy one"[^1].

​The ‌ASCII ​form ‌*lahmu* survives ​only ‌because ​the ​early domain-name ​system ​could ​not ‌carry diacritics; ​it ‌is ​a ‌technological compromise, ​not ‌an ​ancient ‌spelling. The ​Unicode ​restoration ‌**Lahmu** ‌recovers the ‌full ​diacritic ​detail ‌of the ​scholarly ​transliteration ‌directly ​in the ​address ‌bar. ​The ‌restoration needs ​no ​distinctive ​letters ​or diacritics ‌its ‌ASCII ​form ‌would lose, ​which ​places ‌the ‌name in ‌Tier ‌2.

​The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

​- ​**l** ‌→ **L** ​— ​Same, ​capitalized
‌- **a** ​→ ​**a** ​— ‌Same
- ​**h** ‌→ ​**h** ‌— Same
​- ‌**m** ‌→ ​**m** — ​Same
​- ​**u** ‌→ **u** ‌— ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of ‌the name ‌is **/ˈlax.mu/** ​— Akkadian ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ​**La-** — ​Open syllable ‌with short ​[a], from the ​Akkadian root ‌lahāmu, 'to ​be hairy'.
‌- **-ḫ-** ​— Voiceless ‌velar fricative [x], ​written with ​the cuneiform ​ḫu sign ​— the ​consonant that separates ‌Lahmu from ​a simple ‌English h.
​- **-mu** ‌— Bilabial nasal ​[m] plus ‌close back ​vowel [u], ‌the masculine ​nominative ending.

For ​the modern ‌speaker, the ‌closest approximation ‌is: 'LAKH-moo' ​— the middle ​consonant is ‌a dry, ​breathy 'kh' ​like the ‌ch in Scottish ​'loch', not ​a soft ‌English h.

​Kindred and ‌historical forms ​of the name:

​- **Akkadian** ​— 𒀭𒆷𒄷𒈬 ​(dlaḫmu), 'the ‌hairy one' ‌— protective deity ​and primordial ‌figure
- ​**Akkadian feminine** ​— Lahamu ‌(dlaḫmu + feminine ‌-atu), his ‌paired counterpart ‌at the ​threshold
- ‌**Akkadian verb** — ​lahāmu, 'to ​be hairy, ​to be ‌covered with ​hair'

Lahmu is ​Tier 2 ​because the ‌registrable canonical ​form is ​plain ASCII: it ​preserves no ‌distinctive diacritic ​or non-Latin ‌letter. Scholarly ​Assyriological transliteration ‌often writes Laḫmu ​with an ‌underdot ḫ ‌to mark ​the voiceless ​velar fricative, but ​the PuniCodex ​flagship temple ‌displays the ‌unadorned Latin ​form Lahmu.

sections.body:
**Lahmu** ​is the ‌Mesopotamian primordial ‌being whose ​name simply ​means 'the ​hairy one'. ​In the ​*Enuma Elish* ‌he is ​the firstborn ​of Apsû ‌and Tiāmat, ​the earliest ‌divine generation ​before sky ‌and earth ​were fixed. ​Beyond cosmogony, ​he is ​a protective ​spirit: a ‌bearded, hair-covered ​guardian posted ‌at doorways, ​gates, and ‌thresholds to ​turn aside ‌demons and ​pollution.

He ‌stands at ​the border ​between chaos ‌and order ‌— born ‌from the ​mingled primordial ​waters, then ‌stationed at ​the doors ​that keep ‌the ordered ​world safe.[^1]

​### Primordial ‌Firstborn

​First child ‌of Apsû ​and Tiāmat; ​the divine ​line that ​leads to ‌Anshar, Kishar, ‌Anu, and ​Ea begins ‌with him.

​### Guardian ​of the ‌Gate

In ‌ritual and ‌iconography Lahmu ‌protects temple ​and palace ‌doorways, the ​hairy sentinel ​at the ​threshold.

### ‌The Hairy ​One

His ​name and ​form declare ‌the power ​of hair: ​the beard, ​the mane, ‌the shaggy ​pelt that ‌marks the ​apotropaic demon.

‌### Paired ​with Lahamu

‌Lahmu and ‌Lahamu appear ​together as ​a twin ​protective pair, ​male and ‌female guardians ‌of the ​entrance.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Lahmu is ​not a protagonist ‌of long narrative cycles; ‌his power is ​concentrated at origins ​and thresholds. He appears ​at the very ​beginning of the ​Babylonian cosmos, and he ‌endures at the ​edges of the ​ordered world as a ‌guardian.[^1]

### Firstborn ​of the Primordial ‌Waters (Cosmogony)

The ​*Enuma Elish* opens with ‌Apsû, the freshwater ​abyss, and Tiāmat, ​the salt sea. Their ​waters mingled and ​produced the first ​generation of gods: Lahmu ‌and Lahamu, then ​Anshar and Kishar, ‌then Anu, and finally ​Ea (*Enuma Elish* ‌I:1–10). Lahmu is ​therefore the first ‌divine body to emerge ​from chaos, the ‌earliest shape the ​cosmos takes after the ​waters meet.[^2]

### ‌The Hairy Doorkeeper ‌(Apotropaic cult)

In ritual ‌texts and iconography ​Lahmu is a ​protective demon stationed at ‌doorways. His shaggy ​body and beard ​were believed to ‌frighten away evil. Clay ​figurines and glazed ​reliefs show him ‌as a muscular, bearded ​male with curled ‌hair, often flanking ​an entrance. To pass ​his gate was ​to move from ​dangerous outside into ‌protected inside.

### The ‌Six-Curled Guardian (Iconography)

​Lahmu is recognizable ‌in Mesopotamian art by ​his long beard ​arranged in six ‌or seven rounded curls, ‌a naked or ‌lightly clad hairy ‌body, and an aggressive ​stance. He sometimes ‌grasps a weapon ​or a gatepost. ​These attributes made him ​instantly readable as ‌an apotropaic figure: ​the hair that named ​him became the ​visual sign of ‌his power.

### Lahmu ​and Lahamu (Paired ​cult)

Lahmu is ​paired with Lahamu, a ‌feminine counterpart whose ​name shares the ‌same root. Together ​they guard entrances and ‌thresholds, male and ​female aspects of ‌a single protective function. ‌In the *Enuma ​Elish* the pair ​is born together; in ​ritual art they ​are often depicted ‌as matching figures on ‌either side of ​a door.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Lahmu's ​double life ‌— ‌primordial ancestor ​and ​doorway demon ​— ​gave ​him a ‌long ​afterlife in ​Mesopotamian ‌religion.

As ​a ‌cosmogonic figure ​he ‌belongs to ​the ​same watery ​genealogy ​as Apsû ​and ‌Tiāmat, ​and through ‌them ​his memory ‌survives ​in biblical ‌and ​Near Eastern ‌images ​of the ​primordial ‌deep. As ‌a ‌guardian he ​anticipates ​the ‌apotropaic figures ​of ​later traditions: ‌the ​cherubim posted ​at ‌Eden's east ​gate, ‌the lion ​and ​bull colossi ​that ​guard Assyrian ‌palace ‌doors, ​and the ‌sphinxes ​and lamassu ​that ‌still flank ‌temple ‌entrances across ‌the ​ancient Near ‌East. ​The Greek ​daimon ​and the ‌Roman ​genius ​loci partly ​overlap ‌with his ​function, ​though none ​carry ‌his distinctive ​hairy ‌form.[^1]

Within ​the ‌Mesopotamian tradition, ​closely ‌related names ‌in ​the ​corpus include ​[[adad|Adad]], ​[[anu|Anû]], [[apsu|Apsû]], ‌[[ashur|Aššur]], ‌[[dumuzid|Dumuzid]], and ​[[ea|Ēa]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
The ​hairy ‌guardian never ‌fully ​left ​the ​architectural imagination.

​Every ​bearded ‌gatekeeper ​figure, from ​Assyrian ‌palace ​reliefs ‌to medieval ​church ‌gargoyles ​and ​the lion-headed ​knockers ​of ​later ‌doors, preserves ​the ‌old ​idea ‌that a ​threshold ‌needs ​a ‌frightening friend. ​In ​cuneiform ‌studies ‌the name ‌Lahmu ​remains ​a ‌standard example ​of ​how ‌a ​descriptive adjective ​— ‌'the ​hairy ‌one' — ​could ​become ​a ​deity. Modern ‌fantasy ‌and ​games ‌often borrow ​Mesopotamian ​'hairy ‌demons' ‌without knowing ‌their ‌source, ​but ‌the type ​is ​authentically ​ancient. ‌PuniCodex keeps ​the ​plain ​Latin ‌form *Lahmu* ​as ​a ​Tier-2 ‌node: a ​reminder ‌that ​not ‌every restoration ​needs ‌a ‌diacritic; ​some names ​are ​powerful ​precisely ‌because they ‌are ​plain.[^1]

sections.label: Atra-Ḫasīs
sections.body: Although ​Lahmu ‌is ‌not ​named ​as ​a ​speaking ​actor ‌in the ​*Atra-Ḫasīs* ​flood ‌narrative, ​the ‌figure ​belongs ‌to ​the ​same ​Old ​Babylonian ​literary ‌world ​that ‌shaped ​that ‌epic. The ​*Atra-Ḫasīs* ‌describes ​the ‌creation ​of ​human ‌beings ‌from ‌clay ​and ​divine ‌blood ​to ​relieve ‌the ​lesser ​gods ‌of toil; ​Lahmu's ‌own ​clay ​guardian ​images, ​attested ‌in ‌ritual ​texts, ‌echo ​the ​same ‌motif ‌of ‌fashioned ‌beings ​who ‌mediate between ​divine ​and ​human ‌realms. ​The ​pairing ​of ‌primordial ​watery ​origins ​and ‌protective ​bodily ‌form ​links ‌Lahmu ​conceptually to ‌the ‌cosmogonic ​background ​against ​which ​the ‌flood ‌story ​unfolds.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
To ​contemplate ‌Lahmu is ‌to ​hold ​the ​idea ​of primordial ​Being ‌in ​the ​mind ‌and to ​ask ‌what ​of ‌it endures. ​The ​name ​means ​"The ​hairy one"[^1] ‌— ​and ‌a ​name that ‌carries ​its ‌meaning ​so ‌openly invites ​meditation ​rather ‌than ‌mere ‌recollection. The ​tradition ​remembers ‌the ​name as ​primordial ‌Being ​· ​The ‌hairy one.

​Sit ‌with ​the ​restored ​form — ​Lahmu ‌— ‌and ​the diacritics ‌themselves ​become ​the ‌practice: ‌each mark ‌is ‌a ​small ‌act ​of attention, ​a ​refusal ‌to ​let the ​plain ​ASCII ‌form ​*lahmu* ​stand in ​for ‌the ​whole. ‌What the ​tradition ‌preserved ​in ‌this ‌name, the ​restoration ​asks ​the ​reader ‌to preserve ‌in ​turn.
